summary: Describes the Alternate-Marking technique, which measures packet loss, delay, and jitter on live traffic by periodically flipping a marking bit in packets so that counts can be compared between measurement points. It can work with different protocols and can be passive or hybrid. It obsoletes RFC 8321.

plainLanguage.summary: To count lost packets on a live call, two routers have to be counting exactly the same packets at the same moment. The Alternate-Marking Method arranges this by flipping a marking bit in every packet on a timer, so the traffic falls into blocks with alternating colors. Each router counts packets of each color, and the difference between the two counts is the loss.

questions: how to measure packet loss on live traffic
how to measure network delay and jitter passively
how to measure one way delay with marking bits
what is the alternate marking guard band
subtitle: Measure packet loss, delay and jitter on live traffic by flipping a marking bit in packet headers.

tldr.problem: Operators need to measure packet loss, delay and jitter on real traffic. Sequence numbers are hard to use on live traffic, and plain counters at two points cannot be compared unless they cover exactly the same packets.
tldr.mechanism: Packets of a flow are colored with a marking bit that changes on a fixed timer, which splits the flow into blocks. Each measurement point counts and timestamps packets per color, and the results for the same block are compared.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8321 with clarified wording and one-flag and two-flag recommendations, and it MUST only be applied within a controlled domain.

today: RFC 9341 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2022. It obsoletes RFC 8321, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC notes that all of its changes are backward compatible with RFC 8321 and that it introduces no new technique.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Most service providers' networks carry traffic whose contents are highly sensitive to packet loss, delay and jitter. Methodologies and tools are therefore needed to monitor and accurately measure network performance, in order to constantly control the quality of experience perceived by end customers. Performance monitoring also provides useful information for improving network management, such as isolating network problems and troubleshooting.

RFC 7799 defines Active, Passive and Hybrid Methods of Measurement. Active methods depend on a dedicated measurement packet stream, passive methods are based solely on observations of an undisturbed and unmodified packet stream of interest, and hybrid methods combine the two.

This document proposes a performance monitoring technique called the Alternate-Marking Method, which is potentially applicable to any kind of packet-based traffic, both point-to-point unicast and multicast, including Ethernet, IP and MPLS. The method primarily addresses packet-loss measurement, but it can be easily extended to one-way or two-way delay and delay variation measurements as well.

The methodology allows the synchronization of measurements at different points by dividing the packet flow into batches, so it is possible to get coherent counters and timestamps in every marking period. It was designed for passive or hybrid measurements, but under the definitions in RFC 7799 it can be classified as Hybrid Type I, because Alternate Marking can be implemented using reserved bits in the protocol header, and the change in value of those bits at the domain edges is formally considered a modification of the stream of interest.

This is a methodology document, so the mechanism used to transmit the counters and timestamps is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring a live call is harder than measuring a test stream, because you cannot add sequence numbers to packets that are already flowing. This method measures live traffic instead, by coloring packets with a bit that is already in the header.

sections.title: Overview of the Method
sections.content:
The most intuitive way to measure packet loss on a production flow is to number the packets so that each router that receives the flow can immediately detect a missing packet. This is simple in theory but not simple to achieve: it requires inserting a sequence number into each packet, and the devices must be able to extract the number and check it in real time. On live traffic this can be difficult. If UDP is used as the transport protocol the sequence number is not available, and if a higher-layer sequence number such as an RTP header field is used, extracting that information from each packet and processing it in real time could overload the device.

An alternate approach is to count the packets sent at one end, count the packets received at the other end, and compare the two values. This is much simpler to implement, but it requires the devices performing the measurement to be in sync: to compare two counters, they must refer to exactly the same set of packets. Since a flow is continuous and cannot be stopped when a counter has to be read, it can be difficult to determine exactly when to read the counter. A possible solution is to virtually split the flow into consecutive blocks by periodically inserting a delimiter, for example a special packet inserted artificially into the flow. Delimiting the flow with specific packets has limitations: it requires generating additional packets within the flow and requires the equipment to be able to process them, and the method is vulnerable to out-of-order reception of the delimiting packets and, to a lesser extent, to their loss.

The method proposed here follows the second approach, but it does not use additional packets to split the flow into blocks. Instead it marks the packets, so that packets belonging to the same block have the same notional color while consecutive blocks have different colors. Each change of color is a sort of auto-synchronization signal that enhances the consistency of measurements taken by different devices along the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers each keep a packet count. The problem is making sure both counts cover the same packets. The method solves that by giving every packet one of two colors and changing the color on a timer, so both ends can tell where one batch ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Packet-Loss Measurement
sections.content:
The basic idea is to split traffic flows into consecutive blocks, each of which is a measurable entity unambiguously recognizable by all network devices along the path. By counting the packets in each block and comparing the values measured by different devices, it is possible to measure whether packet loss occurred in any single block between any two points.

The traffic is colored with two colors, A and B, so that packets belonging to alternate consecutive blocks have different colors. Whenever the color changes the previous block terminates and the new one begins. The number of packets in each block depends on the criterion used to create it: if the color is switched after a fixed number of packets each block holds the same number of packets, except for any losses, and if the color is switched according to a fixed timer the number of packets may differ per block depending on the packet rate. The use of a fixed timer for the creation of blocks is REQUIRED when implementing this specification.

Traffic coloring can be done by R1 itself if the traffic is not already colored. R1 needs two counters on its egress interface, C(A) and C(B), one counting packets of color A and one counting packets of color B. While the traffic is colored A only the A counter increments, and while it is colored B only the B counter increments. R2 needs the same pair of counters on its ingress interface. When an A block ends it is possible to compare the A counters at the two routers and calculate the loss within that block, and the same is done for each successive block.

Two strategies can be used. The flow-based strategy is used when well-defined flows need to be monitored, so only the specified flow is colored, and it is REQUIRED when implementing this specification. It requires identifying the flow to be monitored and discovering the path it follows; path rerouting and traffic load balancing need to be taken into account. The link-based strategy performs measurements on all the traffic on a link, link by link, and counters may be instantiated for the traffic as a whole or for each traffic class. To have end-to-end monitoring it is enough to enable the monitoring on the first-hop and last-hop routers, because the mechanism is transparent to intermediate nodes. To monitor hop by hop it is necessary to enable the monitoring on every node from source to destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps one counter for each color. When a block ends, the two routers compare their counters for that color, and the difference is the number of packets lost between them.

sections.title: One-Way Delay and Jitter
sections.content:
The same principle used to measure packet loss can be applied to one-way delay. With the single-marking methodology, whenever the color changes a network device stores the timestamp of the first packet of the new block, and that timestamp is compared with the timestamp of the same packet on a second router to compute delay. Because the timestamps refer to specific packets, the first packet of each block, the comparison is valid when there is no packet loss or misordering. A measurement is valid only if no packet loss occurs and packet misordering can be avoided, otherwise the first packet of a block on R1 could differ from the first packet of the same block on R2. Since packet misordering is generally undetectable, this is part of the intrinsic error in the measurement. The clocks on the network nodes must be in sync for the timestamps to be comparable.

A second approach, the mean delay, avoids the sensitivity to out-of-order reception. The device stores a timestamp for each packet received in a block, and the average arrival time for the block is the sum of the timestamps divided by the number of packets received. Subtracting the average arrival times of two adjacent devices gives the mean delay between them. This greatly reduces the number of timestamps collected, one per block per device, and is robust to out-of-order packets with only a small error if packets are lost. It does not give the minimum, maximum and median delay values, and the measurement error can be augmented by accumulating the error of many packets.

The double-marking methodology uses a first marking to create the alternate flow and, within that colored flow, a second marking to select the packets used for measuring delay and jitter. The first marking is needed for packet loss and may be used for mean delay. The second marking creates a set of marked packets that are fully identified over the network, so a device can store their timestamps and compare them with the same packets on the next node. The frequency of the second marking must not be too high, and there should be an adequate time gap between double-marked packets to avoid out-of-order issues, which may at the minimum be the mean network delay. An efficient and robust mode is to select a single packet with the second marking for each block, so there is no time gap to consider and a lost packet is easy to recognise.

The method can also measure inter-arrival jitter, using the definition in RFC 3393. With single marking the alternation of colors acts as the time reference, and with double marking the second-marked packets give the reference. Jitter can be derived from one-way delay measurement by evaluating the delay variation of consecutive samples.
sections.plainLanguage: For delay, the first packet of each block is used as a marker: both routers timestamp it, and the difference is the time the packet took. A second marking picks out individual packets for a more detailed measurement.

sections.title: Alternate-Marking Functions
sections.content:
The coloring operation is fundamental, because it creates the packet blocks and the marked packets, which implies choosing where to activate the coloring and how to color the packets.

For flow-based measurements the flow to monitor can be defined by a set of selection rules such as header fields used to match a subset of the packets, which makes it possible to control the number of nodes involved, the path followed by the packets and the size of the flows. There may be multiple coloring nodes or a single one that is easier to manage and raises no risk of conflict. When several nodes color, the coloring must change periodically between the nodes according to the timing considerations, so every node designated as a measurement point can identify unambiguously the colored packets. It can be advantageous to color the flow as close as possible to the source, because that allows an end-to-end measure if a measurement point is enabled on the last-hop router as well.

For link-based measurements all traffic needs to be colored when transmitted on the link. If it has already been colored it has to be re-colored, because the color must be consistent on the link, so each hop along the path must re-color the traffic. The color is not required to be consistent along different links. Traffic coloring can be implemented by setting specific flags in the packet header and changing the value of that bit periodically; how to choose the marking field depends on the application and is out of scope.

Nodes between source and destination have to count and timestamp the colored packets they receive and forward, and this can be enabled on every router along the path or only on a subset, depending on which network segment is being monitored. Since the color switches periodically between two values, two counters, one for each value, are needed for each flow and for every interface being monitored. The nodes are not able to directly use the counter and timestamp values to measure loss and delay, because they only have their own samples, so the values have to be collected and correlated. Correlation may use a centralized network management system in push or polling mode, or a protocol-based distributed solution that exchanges values between the endpoints, for example by extending TWAMP or OWAMP. An implementation may use a block number for correlation, which must be assigned to each measurement block and associated with each packet count and timestamp reported. This assumes the measurement nodes are time synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone has to decide where the coloring happens and where the counters are read. The counters then have to be brought together somewhere, either in a management system or by a protocol between the routers, so that the two ends of a block can be compared.

sections.title: Synchronization and Timing
sections.content:
Color switching is the reference for all the network devices acting as measurement points. The only requirement is that they recognize the right batch along the path so they can get the related counter and timestamp information.

Clocks in network devices are not accurate, so there is a clock error between measurement points, and to implement the methodology they must be synchronized to the same clock reference with adequate accuracy, so that all devices consistently match the marking bit to the correct block. Packet reordering is also common in a packet network, due to equal-cost multipath, and the delay between measurement points is the main cause of out-of-order packets. If the block is sufficiently large, reordering occurs only at the edge of adjacent blocks and it is easy to assign the reordered packets to the right blocks.

Two contributions therefore have to be taken into account: the clock error between devices and the interval to wait to avoid packets being out of order because of network delay. The RFC assumes all devices are synchronized to a common reference time with an accuracy of plus or minus A/2, so the difference between the clock values of any two devices is bounded by A. The network delay is represented as a normal distribution, with 99.7% of the samples within three standard deviations of the average.

The guard band d is given by d = A + D_avg + 3*D_stddev, where A is the clock accuracy, D_avg is the average network delay between the devices and D_stddev is the standard deviation of the delay. The available counting interval is L - 2d, which must be greater than zero, and the condition that MUST be satisfied is d < L/2, where L is the time duration of each block. Packet counters must be read, and double-marked packets chosen, within the available counting interval, which is not affected by error factors. If the duration of each block is not very small, the synchronization requirement can be met even with a relatively inaccurate synchronization method.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things can spoil a measurement: the routers' clocks disagreeing, and packets arriving late and out of order. The RFC sets a guard band around the end of each block, and the block must be long enough that the safe middle part still exists.

sections.title: Recommendations for Deployment
sections.content:
The only requirement to apply the method is to select and mark the flow to be monitored, so that packets are batched by the sender and each batch is alternately marked such that it can be easily recognized by the receiver. Either one or two flag bits might be available for marking in different deployments. With one flag, packet-loss measurement MUST be done as described in the packet-loss section, and delay measurement MUST be done according to the single-marking methodology. Mean delay MAY also be used, but it could imply more computational load. With two flags, packet-loss measurement MUST be done as described in the packet-loss section, and delay measurement MUST be done according to the double-marking methodology. In that case single marking MAY also be used in combination with double marking, and the two approaches provide slightly different pieces of information that can be combined into a more robust data set.

Several operational guidelines influence the choice. The method uses specific flags in the packet header, so the number of flags available matters: with only one flag there is no other way, and with two flags the option with two flags is more complete. The duration of the marking period affects the frequency of the measurement and can be decided on the basis of the required temporal sampling, but it cannot be freely chosen. The method enables packet loss, delay and delay variation calculation, but the method used determines what information can be derived, and to get more statistics of extent data the option with two flags is desirable. Finally, the different methods imply different computational load, so the resources available on the measurement points can influence the choice.

A deployment must also take into account how to handle and recognize marked and unmarked traffic. Since Alternate Marking normally employs a marking field that is dedicated, reserved and included in a protocol extension, the measurement points can learn whether the measurement is activated by checking whether the specific extension is present in the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: How well you can measure depends on how many spare bits the protocol gives you. One bit gives packet loss and simple delay; a second bit gives a richer delay measurement at a higher processing cost.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document specifies a measurement method that does not directly affect Internet security nor applications that run on the Internet, but implementation must be mindful of security and privacy concerns. There are two types of concern: potential harm caused by the measurements, and potential harm to the measurements.

The measurements are passive, so no new packets are injected into the network. Nevertheless, the method implies modifications on the fly to a header or encapsulation of the data packets, which must be done in a way that does not alter the quality of service experienced by packets subject to measurement and that preserves the stability and performance of the routers doing the measuring. One of the main security threats in operations, administration and maintenance protocols is network reconnaissance, and an attacker can gather information about network performance by passively eavesdropping on those messages. The advantage of the methods described here is that the marking bits are the only information exchanged between the network devices, so passive eavesdropping on data plane traffic does not let attackers learn about network performance.

The measurements could be harmed by routers altering the marking of packets or by an attacker injecting artificial traffic. Authentication techniques such as digital signatures may be used where appropriate to guard against injected traffic attacks. Since routers along the path could intentionally alter marking bits, the mechanism can be applied just in the context of a controlled domain, where the routers are locally administered. An attacker outside the controlled domain can maliciously send marked packets, but no problems occur if Alternate Marking is not supported in the domain. If it is supported, externally marked packets must be checked and eventually filtered or cleared. The precondition for applying the method is that it MUST be applied in specific controlled domains, which confines the potential attack vectors within the network domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The method leaks very little, because the only thing exchanged between routers is a marking bit. The real risk is that someone outside the domain sends fake marked packets, so the domain has to filter them at its edges.

items.title: Block length L
items.text: The time each color lasts. Longer blocks mean less frequent measurements.

items.title: Clock accuracy A
items.text: How far apart the clocks of two measurement points may be.

items.title: Average delay D_avg
items.text: The mean time a packet takes to travel between the two points.

items.title: Delay deviation D_stddev
items.text: How much the delay varies around that average.

items.title: Guard band d
items.text: d = A + D_avg + 3*D_stddev, and it must be less than L/2.

items.title: Counting interval
items.text: L - 2d. This is the part of the block that is safe to read.
